book.title: The Telegraph All New Cryptic Crosswords 4

wordplay.note: a cutlet is a chop, and two of them make a pair of chops

explanation.surface: A diner orders two cutlets and wants them served immediately.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is written as two words, (4,4), one for each cutlet.
explanation.definitionFit: Chop-chop is an informal exclamation urging someone to hurry, meaning right away.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to pay out on a cheque, as a bank does
second meaning: esteem or recognition that does someone good

explanation.surface: A shop assistant asks how the customer will pay.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are taken in less obvious senses: a bank honours a cheque by cashing it, and a person who is a credit to their family is an honour to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Honour as a verb means to pay a cheque; as a noun it means distinction or credit.

clue.text: A gem looks right in a ring

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits inside it, so the second piece goes around the first

parts.note: a ring of church bells is a peal
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A jewel looks just right set in a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The ring is the sound of bells, not jewellery: R goes inside PEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A pearl is a precious gem formed inside an oyster.

parts.note: surface reading: a choice between a woman's name and a town
setter's reading: either part of the word veracity, which means truth, taken alone

explanation.surface: A puzzling choice between a woman named Vera and a city.
explanation.walkthrough: Put the two words together and they make veracity, a word for truth; either one alone is only half of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A half-truth is a statement that tells only part of the facts, as each half of veracity is only part of that word.

clue.text: The sort of hat one may have to eat?

definitions.text: The sort of hat one may have to eat?

parts.words: The sort of hat one may have to eat?
parts.note: surface reading: the idiom of eating one's hat after a wrong prediction

parts.words: The sort of hat one may have to eat?
parts.note: setter's reading: a hat named after a food you can actually eat

explanation.surface: Someone who boasted 'I'll eat my hat' wonders which hat they will have to swallow.
explanation.definitionFit: A pork pie is a flat-crowned hat shaped like the British meat pie it is named after, so it is edible in name.

clue.text: Quiet place for a school break

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a secluded nook or alcove
second meaning: the playtime between lessons

explanation.surface: Someone looks for a calm spot where pupils can spend their break.
explanation.definitionFit: A recess is both a hidden corner of a room and a pause between school lessons.

clue.text: In Australia, football is supreme, O.K.?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Australian ..., the country's own code of football
second meaning: the slogan 'X ..., OK?', saying something is the best

explanation.surface: A fan insists that football reigns supreme in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'X rules, OK' is a British graffiti slogan declaring X the best.
explanation.definitionFit: Aussie Rules is often just called Rules, and to rule is to be supreme.

parts.note: char is British slang for a cup of tea
a lady is a woman

explanation.surface: The woman with the tea trolley turns up every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' is a noun here: in Britain a daily is a cleaning lady who comes in each day.
explanation.definitionFit: A charwoman is a hired cleaner, also called a daily, who comes in to clean houses or offices.

clue.text: Guiding line about two similar points

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first item wraps around the second

parts.note: a string is a line or cord
points are compass points; two the same make E and E

explanation.surface: A guide line runs around two matching points, as in navigation.
explanation.walkthrough: Compass points are N, S, E and W; here the same one, E, is used twice and sits after ST.
explanation.definitionFit: Steering means directing a course, so it is a synonym of guiding.

clue.text: Necessitate being in late for assembly

indicators.note: assembling means putting parts together into a new construction, so these letters are rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Turning up late for school assembly may have consequences.
explanation.definitionFit: To entail something is to involve it as a necessary consequence, so it is a synonym of necessitate.

clue.text: Let out or let out again

definitions.meaning: first meaning: freed, set loose
second meaning: rented out to a tenant once more

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether something was freed or rented a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses of 'let out' differ: freeing a prisoner, and letting property to a tenant, which repeated is re-leasing.
explanation.definitionFit: Released means set free; read as re-leased, it means leased, or rented, to someone again.

clue.text: The mark of a finished writer?

definitions.text: The mark of a finished writer?

parts.words: The mark of a finished writer?
parts.note: surface reading: the sign of an author whose career is over

parts.words: The mark of a finished writer?
parts.note: setter's reading: the punctuation mark a writer puts when a sentence is finished

explanation.surface: It seems to ask what signals that an author has run out of ideas.
explanation.definitionFit: The full stop is the punctuation point that ends a sentence, the mark made when the writing is done.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: people who sew, stitching torn clothes
second meaning: underground drains carrying waste water

explanation.surface: It reads as plumbers at work repairing pipes.
explanation.walkthrough: The word has two pronunciations: those who sew rhyme with 'goers', drains rhyme with 'fluers'.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who sew are sewers, and sewers are also the drains that carry away waste water.

parts.note: Members of Parliament together form the House of Commons
a crowd warming to someone is beginning to cheer them on

explanation.surface: Members of Parliament at a party begin to cheer.
explanation.walkthrough: The House is the House of Commons, the chamber where British MPs sit.
explanation.definitionFit: A housewarming is a party given to celebrate moving into a new home.

clue.text: Upholstery material that is harsh or rough

indicators.note: something rough is crudely or carelessly made, so the letters come out jumbled

parts.note: i.e. is the Latin abbreviation for 'that is'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A stuffing for furniture that feels harsh and rough to sit on.
explanation.definitionFit: Horsehair, hair from a horse's mane or tail, was the traditional stuffing for chairs and sofas.

clue.text: Battle to get a gang leader on trial

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the leader of a group is at its front, so take only the opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of gang
someone on trial is in court

explanation.surface: Prosecutors battle to get a gang boss into the dock.
explanation.definitionFit: Agincourt is the battle of 1415 in which Henry V's English army defeated the French.

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means read from bottom to top, so the word is turned round

parts.note: pop and pa are both informal words for father
to boost someone is to talk them up or praise them

explanation.surface: A pop-up promotion meant to raise a product's value.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop up' looks like one verb; Pop is father and up turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: To appraise something is to value it, that is, to estimate its worth.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: anxious dread about what may happen
second meaning: the capture of a suspect by police

explanation.surface: A fugitive dreads being caught.
explanation.definitionFit: Apprehension is anxiety about the future, and the apprehension of a suspect is the act of seizing them.

indicators.note: something made new is changed from its old form, so the letters take another order

parts.note: taken as written
the four compass points divide the compass into quarters; E for east is one

explanation.surface: A newcomer living in the native quarter of a town shows innocence.
explanation.definitionFit: Naivety is innocent, unworldly lack of sophistication, the kind of simplicity of an inexperienced person.

clue.text: Sarcastic driver on course put in charge

parts.note: on a golf course, the clubs that drive the ball include irons
i/c is the standard abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A mocking chauffeur on a racecourse is put in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driver' suggests a motorist; on a golf course it is a club, and an iron is another club for hitting the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironic speech says the opposite of what is meant in a mocking way, close to sarcastic.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: halt, bring to a standstill
second meaning: a step in a criminal case, when police detain a suspect

explanation.surface: It seems to ask how to halt a criminal trial already under way.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrest is to stop something, and an arrest is the first proceeding taken against a suspected criminal.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an ugly giant of Scandinavian folklore
second meaning, as a verb: to fish by trailing a baited line behind a boat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' reads as a noun after 'Monster', but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A troll is a folklore monster living under bridges, and to troll is to fish with a moving line.

indicators.note: read as re-sort, it tells us to put these letters in a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hidden holiday spot in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a noun for a holiday place, but split as re-sort it is the signal to rearrange the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: In camera is a legal phrase for proceedings held in private, so it means secret.

parts.note: surface reading: organisations such as Reuters that sell reports to papers
setter's reading: the means through which news reaches the public

explanation.definitionFit: The media are the newspapers, radio and television, the plural channels through which news is passed on.

parts.note: surface reading: a spoken exam in the Latin language
setter's reading: the Latin phrase used for a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A student faces a spoken exam in Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin is in the answer, not the subject of the exam: the phrase means 'with the living voice'.
explanation.definitionFit: A viva voce, often just a viva, is an oral examination, especially of a university thesis.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: brought to ruin, finished
second meaning: left incomplete, never carried out

explanation.surface: A condemned person is ruined but escapes the gallows.
explanation.definitionFit: Undone describes someone destroyed, and also a task that has not been done or carried out.

parts.note: surface reading: a cultured, well-mannered train driver
setter's reading: something produced in a refinery that drives an engine

explanation.surface: It paints a genteel, well-spoken locomotive driver.
explanation.definitionFit: Petrol is fuel refined from crude oil, and it powers a car's motor.

definitions.meaning: first meaning, stressed on the second syllable: to enchant
second meaning, stressed on the first syllable: a door or gate

explanation.surface: Someone uses charm to get admitted somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance is to fill with delight, and an entrance is the door by which one gets into a place.
